# The Deep End of the Ordinary

Pick up the nearest small object. A pen, a paperclip, a spoon. It feels like a simple thing, but that's an illusion born of familiarity. Hold it long enough and it starts to deepen, like one of those magic-eye pictures, except what emerges is real.

Consider the paperclip. The standard Gem-style clip—that elegant double loop—was perfected around 1899 and never meaningfully improved. Humanity has landed probes on comets and taught sand to do arithmetic, but nobody has found a better way to fasten paper together with a bit of bent wire. The clip is steel, which means iron dug from a specific hole in the ground, alloyed, drawn into wire, cut, and folded by machines whose entire purpose on Earth is performing this one small gesture, millions of times a day. And during the Nazi occupation of Norway, people wore paperclips on their lapels as a quiet signal: *we are bound together*. A fastening device, doing its job at national scale.

Or take bread. We tend to assume agriculture came first and baking followed, but the evidence suggests the opposite. At a site in Jordan called Shubayqa, archaeologists found charred flatbread crumbs made by hunter-gatherers roughly 14,400 years ago—thousands of years before anyone planted a field. It's entirely possible that the craving for bread is what lured us into farming in the first place; that we didn't domesticate grain so much as grain, through the medium of toast, domesticated us. And a sourdough starter is a whole other rabbit hole: a living ecosystem of wild yeast and bacteria, maintained by bakers for decades, passed hand to hand like a pet that happens to make breakfast.

Language is full of this kind of hidden depth. The word *window* comes from the Old Norse *vindauga*—"wind-eye." Every time you glance out a window you're using an eye for the wind. English is a sedimentary rock of fossilized metaphors, and once you start noticing them it's hard to stop. *Consider* apparently contains the Latin *sidus*, star—to consider something is, etymologically, to sit with the stars, probably a leftover from some augur reading the sky. Which means that even ordinary thought carries a faint memory of astronomy.

Then there are pigeons, which might be the most misunderstood animals on the planet. Here's the thing people don't realize: pigeons are not wild birds that adapted to cities. They're domestic animals we abandoned. Every pigeon strutting down a sidewalk is a rock dove descended from centuries of careful breeding—for food, for racing, for carrying messages. We built them, essentially, and then the telephone made them obsolete and we just left them outside. They keep choosing to live near us anyway, which is either touching or embarrassing depending on your mood. And they were good at their jobs: a pigeon named Cher Ami flew through gunfire in 1918 to save nearly two hundred trapped soldiers, and more than thirty pigeons received medals for gallantry in the Second World War. The animal you're shooing away from your fries has decorated war heroes in its family tree.

Even shadows turn out to be weirder than advertised. On a sunny day, stand under a leafy tree and look at the dappled light on the ground. Those little circles aren't leaf-shaped holes—they're images of the sun itself. Each gap between leaves works as a pinhole camera, projecting the sun's disc onto the pavement. During a partial eclipse, every one of those dapples becomes a tiny crescent, thousands of copies of the eclipse scattered at your feet. Most people walk right over a pavement full of suns without ever knowing it.

This is the part that genuinely interests me: the transformation isn't in the world, it's in the observer. Before you know about the pinhole effect, a tree's shadow is just shade. Afterward, it's an optical instrument, and you can't unsee it. A birdwatcher walking through a park is visiting a different park than everyone else—where you see "some birds," they see a dozen distinct species with names, habits, and dramas in progress. Someone who learns to identify trees will tell you the experience is startling: a street that used to be lined with generic greenery suddenly becomes a crowd of specific individuals. There's even a term for the before-state: plant blindness. The world was always detailed. We just weren't reading it.

I find this quietly radical, because it means boredom is rarely the world's fault. It's usually a resolution problem—a failure of zoom. Everything boring is boring only at one particular distance. Move closer and the spoon becomes metallurgy and trade routes; move further out and it becomes part of a ritual of eating that humans have been performing around fires for hundreds of thousands of years. There is no scale at which a thing fully exhausts itself.

The other hopeful implication is that attention is a skill rather than a fixed trait. You can practice it the way you'd practice anything. Learn the names of five trees and your neighborhood changes. Learn one etymology a week and your own language starts glowing at the seams. Ask one dumb question about an ordinary object—why is the paperclip shaped like that, where did this bread come from, what *is* a pigeon, anyway—and you're immediately standing at the edge of something much larger than the question.

None of this costs anything. That's the almost suspicious generosity of it. The depth was there the whole time, folded into the least impressive objects in your vicinity, no ticket required.

So: pick up the nearest small object again. It's still just a paperclip or a spoon. But now maybe you can feel it—that slight vertigo, the sense that there's no bottom to it, that the ordinary was always the deep end. Everything is like this. Everything is more than it appears, patiently waiting for someone to look twice.

The looking is the whole trick. And it's available constantly, for free, forever.

I could write about:

- Something about language and how strange it is
- The experience of reading or thinking
- An observation about the world
- Time, memory, attention
- The strange intimacy of text conversations
- Something philosophical but grounded

Let me think about what I'd actually want to write about if given free rein. One thing that strikes me as genuinely fascinating is the phenomenon of "threshold moments"—those liminal experiences like standing in a doorway, or the moment before sleep, or waiting rooms. Actually, let me write about something I find genuinely captivating: the idea that the world is full of hidden depths in ordinary things. The way a cup of coffee contains geology, agriculture, trade routes, chemistry, personal memory. How expertise reveals invisible layers. How a walk through a city is different for an architect vs. a birdwatcher vs. a historian. Or I could write about reading—what it actually is, this strange technology of marks on a page becoming voices in the head. That's genuinely weird when you think about it.

Let me combine some threads: I want to write about attention and the layered nature of ordinary reality. Maybe frame it around the idea that ordinary things are portals—that anything examined closely enough becomes strange and wonderful.
